newsitem.title: FRANCE: Grain--How EU storage aid plan would affect prices.
newsitem.headline: Grain--How EU storage aid plan would affect prices.

text.p: A European Commission proposal to reduce monthly grain storage aid by nine percent would shave around a dollar a tonne from French wheat exports if applied to current prices, grain traders said.
The proposal for 1997/98 (July/June) does not in fact apply to current old-crop prices, but the difference of about a dollar serves as an illustration of its effect.
The EU's executive, in an annual bid to reduce grain storage incentives, proposed in a price package on Wednesday to cut the monthly increment to one Ecu per tonne from 1.1 Ecus now.

French traders buy grain on a "July" basis, with storage adjustments stripped out. They then add on a sum equating to half the value of the EU's monthly increment for every half-month elapsing between August 1 and the delivery date.
Converted into francs at the EU's agrimoney green rate, the storage increment for first-half March is 54.53 francs a tonne.
To illustrate the change, if the new proposal applied to the current season, the premium would be 49.58 francs instead.
On an export basis, using the latest EU refund of 12.90 Ecus per tonne, prompt fob French wheat would then be worth some $151.75 a tonne instead of $152.75 at present, traders reckoned.
The calculation is purely for comparison since the value of EU export refunds traded on the open market has fallen sharply since last Thursday's weekly export tender.
Exporters in turn receive the EU storage aid in whole monthly steps from Brussels when using export licences issued at least one month before they are actually used.
For grain traders, the EU move was largely expected and represented an annual bid by the Commission to cut what it regards as generous incentives to store grain.
"This seems reasonable. It is what you would expect, although the whole increment system is rather old-fashioned anyway," said one senior French trader.
Critics of the system say it disrupts markets at times of tight supply while its backers say it smooths out grain supplies over the crop marketing year.
The Commission has frequently attempted to cut the storage bonus as low as possible.
It argues that when the increments are compared with modern low interest rates, they offer too much financial cushioning to farmers and their cooperatives.
But European Union farm ministers have usually resisted efforts to cut the storage aid too sharply.
Ministers are due to decide on the Commission's annual price-fixing proposals by the end of June.
The Commission is also proposing to leave basic cereals intervention prices unchanged at 119.19 Ecus a tonne.
But it wants to cut compensatory payments to cereals farmers by 7.3 percent to 50.37 Ecus a tonne.
